item.title: Driver Kills Two College Cyclists in Tennessee, Officials Say
item.description:
A driver was charged with vehicular homicide on Wednesday after officials said he struck members of a college cycling team, killing two, as they were training on a mountain highway in northeast Tennessee.

The crash happened around 9 a.m., when the driver of a passenger car struck members of the Milligan University cycling team on Highway 19 near Simerly Creek Road in Carter County, Tenn., officials said.

Milligan University, a Christian school in Milligan, Tenn., near Johnson City, said that two sophomores, Haylan Engdahl and Brayden Rogers, were killed. Seven other members of the cycling team were taken to Johnson City Medical Center, two of them by helicopter.

Four of the students were in critical condition in the surgical intensive care unit Wednesday evening; two were stable in condition; and one was released, Dr. Bracken Burns, the trauma medical director at Johnson City Medical Center, said at a news conference.

In an emotional video message, Stephen Waers, the president of Milligan University, asked for prayers from the campus community and said that pastors and counselors would be available to assist grieving students.

“We need to be gathered together, gathered together around Jesus, and we need to help our brothers and sisters bear burdens that are too great for any one person to carry alone,” he said.

Eleven Milligan University cyclists were on a training ride together when the crash occurred, Mr. Waers said.

Maj. Roy Brown of the Tennessee Highway Patrol said at a news conference on Wednesday afternoon that a large number of emergency workers responded to the scene. Officials declined to release details about the crash, which Major Brown said remained under investigation.

The speed limit on that part of the road is 50 miles per hour, according to the Tennessee Department of Transportation.

“We know the families and Milligan University deeply want answers, and we want to provide those answers,” Major Brown said.

Steven R. Finney, the district attorney general for Carter County, said that the driver, John Benfield, 69, of Newland, N.C., had been charged with two counts of vehicular homicide by recklessness and five counts of aggravated assault by vehicle by recklessness. He said Mr. Benfield was being booked into jail.

“This is an elite cycling team,” Mr. Finney said. “It’s not a bunch of those club guys getting together to ride. They know what they’re doing. They rode in a peloton. One of the boys just won last weekend in one of the local races.”

Milligan University, which has about 1,200 students, is about 11 miles from the scene of the crash in the Blue Ridge Mountains.

In May, the university announced that its cycling team had won the men’s team time trial national championship at the U.S.A. Cycling Collegiate Road Nationals in Madison, Wis.

item.title: In Wyoming’s G.O.P. Primaries, an Emphatic Rebuke of the Hard Right
item.description:
The ultraconservatives in Wyoming’s Freedom Caucus entered Tuesday’s Republican primaries with visions of a clean sweep of the state government, from the governor’s office to the State Senate and House.

Instead, the pendulum swung the other way — hard.

Republican voters in Wyoming rejected Freedom Caucus candidates who ran for governor, secretary of state and schools superintendent, siding with more mainstream conservative Republicans, The Associated Press reported.

In the primary to succeed the low-key outgoing governor, Mark Gordon, State Senator Eric Barlow, a rancher and veteran lawmaker, topped Megan Degenfelder, the schools superintendent who was endorsed by President Trump, and another hard-right candidate, Brent Bien, a retired Marine colonel backed by the Wyoming Republican Party.

At least a dozen Freedom Caucus incumbents were ousted from the Legislature, possibly including three of the four leaders of the caucus in the State House. (With 99 percent of the votes counted, one leader lost soundly, and two others were behind, including Chip Neiman, the House speaker who was running for State Senate.)

Rather than seizing control of the state’s upper chamber, the Freedom Caucus lost its majority in the House.

The results — a “near-total massacre,” as Wyoming’s Cowboy State Daily put it — were a stinging rebuke of the hard-right agenda and aggressive style that had propelled Wyoming in 2024 to become the country’s first such caucus to control a statehouse chamber.

The caucus had used that power to expand a voucher program to pay private school tuition and make Wyoming the first state to ban abortion pills, a law struck down by the State Supreme Court. But without a majority in the State Senate, it failed to enact deep cuts to the University of Wyoming, gut the state’s economic development office or the revamp the judiciary — prompting Mr. Neiman and others to run for Senate.

“Wyoming citizens spoke loud and clear tonight!” State Representative Landon Brown, a Republican and frequent Freedom Caucus critic, wrote on Facebook. “They want TRUE governance, not child’s play.”

Tuesday night’s winners now advance to November’s general election. Most will be heavily favored against Democrats in a Republican state that delivered President Trump his biggest margin of victory in 2024.

The wipeout of far-right candidates did not extend to federal offices. Harriet Hageman, who ousted one of Mr. Trump’s fiercest Republican critics, Liz Cheney, to take Wyoming’s lone U.S. House seat in 2022, on Tuesday easily won the Republican primary to succeed retiring U.S. Senator Cynthia Lummis. Chuck Gray, the current secretary of state, emerged first in a hard-fought, expensive and crowded primary to replace Ms. Hageman in the U.S. House.

But Cheyenne was another story.

In the Legislature, five state representatives who have identified with the Freedom Caucus tried to unseat more traditional Republicans in the State Senate. Three lost outright. And in the most highly anticipated showdown, Mr. Neiman, who represents a district in the shadow of the Devils Tower national monument, was trailing State Senator Ogden Driskill, a self-described “Reagan conservative” who has been office since 2011.

In another notable race, State Representative Rachel Williams, the Freedom Caucus chairwoman who had urged Governor Gordon to join the fight against certifying President Biden’s victory in 2020, lost her bid for secretary of state, the state’s top elections official. Voters sided with Robert Short, a county official who has praised local election officials and volunteers for doing “a spectacular job.”

State Representative John Bear, a former Freedom Caucus chairman, was trailing Doug Moore, a coal industry manager and political newcomer who pledged to focus on deregulation. Mr. Moore was backed by Americans for Prosperity, a veteran conservative group, and Common Sense Republicans, a new organization that had warned that an empowered Freedom Caucus would enact deep cuts to schools and law enforcement.

Americans for Prosperity opposed numerous Freedom Caucus legislative candidates, but its spending was dwarfed by Make Liberty Win, a pro-Freedom Caucus political action committee.

Make Liberty Win and other groups prioritized defeating Mr. Barlow in the governor’s race. But he won handily after promising to lower the temperature of Wyoming’s politics, and work on bread-and-butter issues such as energy, rural health care and water.

In one memorable video referring to the negative mailers inundating voters, Mr. Barlow — who is also a veterinarian — pulled on a long plastic veterinarian’s glove, reached into his mailbox and retrieved a pile of yak dung.

item.title: Alabama Democrats Look for a Black Backlash Over Voting Rights
item.description:
Doug Jones, a former senator, and Shomari Figures, a current but endangered representative, have been here before in Alabama.

Mr. Jones lost his Senate seat in 2020 to Tommy Tuberville, a former college football coach, and now hopes to beat him in November in a contest for governor. Mr. Figures won a House district in 2024 that was redrawn to give Black voters more representation. Now he is confronting new district lines drawn explicitly to give his seat to a Republican.

Besides being Democrats, what both men have in common is a need for Alabama’s Black voters to come out in November in overwhelming numbers, energized and angered in part by the Supreme Court’s decision in April that weakened the Voting Rights Act and set off a new wave of redistricting in the South.

“They know that their vote is not counting the same way,” Mr. Jones said of Black voters in an interview before a town hall in Troy, Ala., on Tuesday. He added, “People are paying attention to that, and they’re not happy about it.”

Voting rights are deeply personal in Alabama, where the state’s white leaders spent the civil rights movement strenuously resisting their Black citizens’ demands for a fair shake at the ballot box. The blood of those citizens helped galvanize Washington to enact the Voting Rights Act in 1965.

Then this spring, acting on a lawsuit in Louisiana, the Supreme Court freed Southern leaders from the act’s strictures encouraging minority representation. Tennessee, Louisiana and Alabama all moved quickly to dilute districts with strong blocs of Black voters and tilt them toward the G.O.P.

Alabama’s Legislature redrew the Second Congressional District where Mr. Figures’s victory in 2024 gave the state two Black House members — Mr. Figures and Representative Terri Sewell — for the first time.

“Two was like giving candy to a baby — we were so happy, so excited,” said Gwendolyn Davis, 67, as she prepared to leave the Troy town hall with a stack of yard signs. “And with one stroke of a pen from another state, the Supreme Court has reversed” that.

She added, “I will do whatever I can to make sure that people realize how important it is.”

The new Second District was drawn to favor Republicans by pairing the majority-Black city of Montgomery with part of the southeastern Wiregrass region, making the new district whiter and more conservative. The old lines had stretched farther across the state, linking voters in Montgomery and part of Mobile to voters in the rural counties once farmed by slaves.

Both Mr. Tuberville and Rhett Marques, a Republican state representative running against Mr. Figures, supported the new congressional map and are favored to win their races.

Their campaigns, both backed by Mr. Trump, have worked to frame their Democratic opponents as extreme and out of touch. In a primary election night speech this month, Mr. Marques described the election as a choice between “craziness and common sense.”

But Democrats say they have a chance, predicting that a backlash over the new congressional maps will energize Black voters as President Trump’s sagging approval ratings demoralize white conservatives, many of who might sit the election out.

That Democratic hope goes beyond Alabama and other Southern states directly affected by the voting rights decision. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee on Wednesday launched digital advertisements in New York, Nebraska and Ohio House districts aimed at mobilizing Black voters, some of them explicitly invoking voting rights and the need for representation. Those ads followed a civil-rights-themed blitz last May in 21 House districts.

There is evidence that Black voters are indeed energized, though not necessarily over voting rights. In Wisconsin’s Democratic primary for governor last week, David Crowley, Milwaukee County’s Black executive, scored an astounding upset over a democratic socialist, Francesca Hong, who had been leading comfortably in the polls but struggling with Black voters. Black Milwaukee may well have made the difference.

A similar story played out in Michigan earlier this month, where Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive physician running for Senate, seemed to be cruising to a Democratic primary victory, despite troubles with Black voter support. In the end, he barely squeaked out a win over Representative Haley Stevens, who defied the polls and nearly scored an upset with Black support in Detroit and Flint.

For Mr. Jones and Mr. Figures, the civil rights theme is not a stretch. As a U.S. attorney in Birmingham, Mr. Jones helped prosecute two members of the Ku Klux Klan who bombed a church there in 1963 and killed four young Black girls.

Mr. Figures’s father, Michael Figures, a state senator and civil rights lawyer, helped bring the lawsuit that bankrupted the Klan. Michael Figures also helped sue the state of Alabama over its congressional map in the 1990s, leading to the creation of the first majority-Black district in the state.

This campaign season, Mr. Figures and Mr. Jones have linked arms, joining each other in Troy and Montgomery for town halls this month where they challenged their state leaders.

“They have to do everything they can to reduce representation,” Mr. Figures told the crowd in a ballroom at Troy University.

“They redrew my district in furtherance of that effort,” he said. “But we’re going to win it in November.”

Mr. Jones has campaigned in several majority-Black counties, including rural Greene County, which has already shown signs of the energy that he will need. About 79 percent of Greene County is Black, and in the May primary, turnout was strikingly high.

Last month, Mr. Jones told a cluster of residents gathered at the Greene County courthouse that Alabama leaders were “going to draw district lines to make sure” that “your voice is not represented in the Congress of the United States.”

“I think the Voting Rights Act is going to be an issue in this fall campaign,” Mr. Jones added. “And I think people are energized.”

Such sentiments carry risk. Some organizers cautioned that the new maps could also demoralize Black Alabamians already disconnected from political leaders. Energizing such voters will not happen automatically.

“Each time that you take people’s rights away like that, they’re going to be discouraged and they’re not going to want to go vote,” said Marilyn Hobbs, who volunteers with a voter education organization in Montgomery. “We’ve got to knock on the doors.”

item.title: Trump to Appear on Radio With Michael Cohen, His Onetime Nemesis
item.description:
President Trump has called Michael D. Cohen a “rat” and a “liar.” Mr. Cohen, the president’s former personal lawyer and fixer, has likened Mr. Trump to a mobster.

Now they are poised to formally — and publicly — bury the hatchet.

Mr. Trump is expected to call into a radio show Mr. Cohen is hosting on Thursday, capping one of the more stunning rapprochements of the Trump era.

The conversation, scheduled to air on a Trump-friendly station in New York, WABC, comes nearly eight years to the day that Mr. Cohen pleaded guilty to federal crimes and implicated Mr. Trump in the same wrongdoing.

It also comes more than two years after Mr. Cohen served as the star witness at Mr. Trump’s criminal trial in New York State Court, delivering testimony that helped secure the then-former president’s conviction for falsifying business records related to a hush-money deal with a porn star.

Their planned radio appearance was first reported by MS NOW.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In a text message on Wednesday, Mr. Cohen said that Mr. Trump would call into WABC on Thursday, and that their conversation would air at 6 p.m.

It will mark their first public appearance together since their relationship crumbled during Mr. Trump’s first term. They met briefly last year at the president’s private, members-only golf club in Bedminster, N.J., breaking a yearslong estrangement, The New York Times reported.

More recently, as Mr. Cohen sought to make peace with his former boss, he renounced his cooperation with the prosecutors who brought charges against Mr. Trump.

Mr. Cohen, who once vowed to help prosecutors hold Mr. Trump “accountable for his dirty deeds,” now contends that he “felt compelled and coerced to deliver what they were seeking.” He also accused prosecutors of posing “inappropriate leading questions to elicit answers that supported their narrative.”

After issuing that criticism in January, Mr. Cohen met with Mr. Trump in Florida. By the summer, with the White House’s apparent blessing, Mr. Cohen debuted a radio show on WABC. He said Mr. Trump would eventually join him as a guest.

It is unclear what they will discuss on air on Thursday, but in a text message on Wednesday, Mr. Cohen promoted it like a prime-time exclusive.

“Two old friends separated by time, betrayal, and the world’s biggest spotlight…sit down, face to face,” Mr. Cohen wrote. “It’s time to talk.”

Shawn McCreesh contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump, Who Has Amassed Enormous Wealth in Crypto, Hosts Industry Leaders
item.description:
President Trump met with crypto executives at the White House on Wednesday, voicing his support for an industry that has generated enormous wealth for him and his family and calling on Congress to pass a major cryptocurrency bill.

Mr. Trump convened the group in the Roosevelt Room, where he reeled off the names of his industry visitors, some of whom are business partners of his family’s crypto company.

“Great group of people,” Mr. Trump said as he surveyed the room. “Tremendous investors, brilliant people.”

Officially, the meeting was a kickoff event for a new “innovation advisory committee,” a group of business leaders assembled to advise the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, one of the regulatory agencies that oversees crypto. But it was also a vivid display of Mr. Trump’s tangled relationship with the crypto industry, a business that brought in $1.4 billion for him last year, creating enormous conflicts of interest.

Among the attendees was Sergey Nazarov, the co-founder of Chainlink, a company that formed a partnership last year with the Trump family’s crypto start-up, World Liberty Financial. Another executive, Mike Belshe, heads BitGo, a World Liberty partner that Mr. Trump described at the meeting as “a big deal.”

Also in the room were Brian Armstrong, the founder of the crypto exchange Coinbase, and Arjun Sethi, the chief executive of the Kraken exchange. Both companies offer venues for buying and selling several coins launched by the Trumps. The White House and World Liberty have repeatedly denied any conflicts of interest.

“The New York Times apparently thinks the president of the United States praising the leaders of well-known American companies is a controversy,” said David Wachsman, a World Liberty spokesman.

Mr. Trump met with the executives at a high-stakes moment in the crypto world. The industry’s top priority is the passage of a bill called the Clarity Act, which would create business-friendly rules for the technology. In recent weeks, the bill has faced hurdles in the Senate, where Democrats have pushed for language that would bar public officials, including the president, from selling digital currencies.

At the White House meeting, Mr. Trump steered clear of the major questions surrounding the legislation. But he called on Congress to pass the Clarity Act, describing it as “very, very powerful structured legislation, which will keep us ahead of China.”

A onetime crypto skeptic, Mr. Trump embraced the technology on the campaign trail in 2024 and soon turned it into a cornerstone of his family business. Last year, the Securities and Exchange Commission ended a long-running crackdown, dropping lawsuits against some of the largest crypto firms, including Coinbase and Kraken.

Mr. Trump also signed a bill called the GENIUS Act, which he joked on Wednesday he had named for himself. The law created rules for stablecoins, a popular cryptocurrency tied to the U.S. dollar.

But lately the industry has run into problems in Washington.

For years, crypto executives have lobbied Congress to create a broad regulatory framework governing the industry. The aim was to cement some of Mr. Trump’s pro-crypto policy changes, ensuring that a future president would be unable to reverse them.

A version of the Clarity Act passed the House of Representatives last year, with support from Democrats and Republicans. So far, however, the Senate has not held a vote, because Democrats have demanded tougher rules to stop Mr. Trump from profiting from crypto.

As the executives gathered at the White House on Wednesday, Democrats in Congress were voicing outrage over a new commingling of the interests of the Trump family’s business with the administration’s duties.

Last week, a Treasury Department office granted an affiliate of World Liberty preliminary approval for a limited bank charter. The president and his sons have a hefty stake in World Liberty. The Treasury’s Office of the Comptroller of the Currency supervises banks.

A charter would save World Liberty money by allowing it to issue its stablecoin on its own. Right now, it pays BitGo to do that. The license would not allow it to take deposits from retail customers or issue loans.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, called the pending charter “the most brazen act of self-dealing our financial system has ever seen” and said she would introduce a bill to try to stop it.

Anna Kelly, a White House spokeswoman, denied that a bank charter for World Liberty would present any conflict of interest. “This is the same tired narrative that Democrats have pushed against President Trump, his family and his administration for a decade,” she said. “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public.”

At the meeting, crypto executives celebrated some of their recent victories, including a push from the S.E.C. to give them new leeway to raise capital without federal oversight.

The agency on Tuesday proposed rules that would allow companies to raise up to $75 million per year without registering. Generally, businesses are required to register with the S.E.C. to solicit funds from investors.

The S.E.C. chairman, Paul Atkins, stood alongside Mr. Trump at the White House. “We’re all happy with Paul,” Mr. Trump said from the lectern. “He’s been absolutely fantastic.”

As the session ended, Mr. Trump led the visiting crypto executives into the Oval Office.

“We’re going to show them a real office,” he said. “Their offices are nice, but this is nicer.”

item.title: Senate Health Panel Chairman Voices Strong Reservations About F.D.A. Nominee
item.description:
The chairman of the Senate health committee on Wednesday expressed “strong concerns” about President Trump’s nominee to lead the Food and Drug Administration, criticizing her support of what he called a “nonsensical vaccine executive order” issued last week.

“That alone is almost disqualifying,” the chairman, Senator Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana Republican, wrote on social media.

The senator made his comments hours after Mr. Trump announced he had nominated Dr. Heidi Overton, a White House domestic policy official, to fill the vacancy left by Dr. Marty Makary, who resigned from the F.D.A. in May. Mr. Cassidy’s post was an immediate signal that Dr. Overton could face trouble getting confirmed.

Dr. Overton must win approval from the health committee for her nomination to advance to a full Senate vote. To do that, she will most likely need the support of every Republican on the panel.

The White House quickly defended Dr. Overton. A spokesman, Kush Desai, said Dr. Overton had “spent the last year and a half coordinating an interagency policymaking process with senior officials” to deliver on the administration’s Make America Healthy Again agenda.

“The White House looks forward to her swift confirmation by the Senate,” Mr. Desai said.

But the selection of Dr. Overton also drew complaints from some MAHA leaders, who are upset with the president over an executive order he issued earlier this year aimed at expanding the production of glyphosate, a weedkiller manufactured by Bayer that some scientists have linked to cancer.

Kelly Ryerson, an environmental activist who has accused the Trump administration of being “entirely owned by Bayer and the chemical companies,” said in a text message that she opposed Dr. Overton’s nomination. Ms. Ryerson was among several MAHA leaders who were invited to the White House in April to meet with Mr. Trump and his aides in an effort to smooth over tensions about glyphosate production.

“When I was at the White House MAHA meeting, Overton delivered all of Bayer’s talking points,” Ms. Ryerson said. “She is how corporate capture will thrive at the F.D.A. and is an enemy of MAHA, perpetuating chemical poisoning of the American people.”

The Senate is in recess until mid-September, and Mr. Cassidy has not said whether or when he will hold a confirmation hearing on Dr. Overton’s nomination. Mr. Cassidy, a physician, is a strong proponent of vaccination, and he has repeatedly accused Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. of sowing doubts about vaccine safety.

In his social media post, Mr. Cassidy faulted Dr. Overton for appearing to fuel such doubts. She stood beside Mr. Trump last week during the signing of a third executive order calling for fewer childhood vaccinations; the order has no legal power and has been broadly criticized by public health experts.

“While I respect Dr. Overton’s experience as a physician, I have strong concerns about her nomination to be FDA Commissioner,” Mr. Cassidy wrote. “Her lack of managerial experience does not prepare her well for leading a large organization that is already dealing with staffing and morale issues.”

“Additionally,” he wrote, “Dr. Overton’s active role in last week’s nonsensical vaccine executive order calls into question her commitment to standing up for sound science and protecting children’s health.”

item.title: Trump Officials Scrap Effort to Recruit Pentagon Lawyers to Represent Migrant Children
item.description:
The Trump administration on Wednesday abruptly scrapped a plan to recruit retiring Pentagon lawyers to represent unaccompanied minors in immigration court, a move that would have asked attorneys with little relevant legal experience to help migrant children facing deportation.

The shift deepened confusion about how the federal government planned to fulfill its legal obligation to protect the rights of the more than 20,000 unaccompanied minors with pending immigration cases, who advocates say are uniquely vulnerable amid the administration’s push for mass expulsions.

A federal contract with a network of legal nonprofit groups that had long represented unaccompanied minors ended last month. The Trump administration signed a short-term deal earlier this month with an organization best known for its focus on human trafficking, an arrangement that would provide the children with lawyers. Opponents of the move have noted that the group, Our Rescue, has little experience handling immigration court cases.

The administration had also been developing another stopgap measure. Officials with the Defense Department and the Health and Human Services Department, which is responsible for the welfare of migrant children who have no parent or legal guardian to care for them in the United States, told The New York Times earlier this week that the administration was recruiting Pentagon lawyers who had recently retired or had planned to retire soon to serve as attorneys for the children.

Such an arrangement would have been a departure from the kind of work typically provided by Pentagon lawyers, who have experience on a broad array of matters for the civilian and military branches of the armed services. That includes prosecuting or defending service members in courts-martial, reviewing contracts for new weapons and ensuring troops follow the laws of armed conflict.

By Wednesday afternoon, as The Times sought more information from H.H.S., the department said it was no longer pursuing the idea, which had not been disclosed publicly.

The agency said that for now, it would use short-term contracts to provide migrant children with lawyers in immigration court. It acknowledged that the administration was still seeking to identify a long-term legal service provider.

The department said in a statement that it remained “committed to ensuring all eligible unaccompanied children have legal representation during immigration proceedings.”

While immigrant advocates expressed relief that the plan to tap military lawyers was tossed, they said the patchwork plan to provide legal services could lead to more deportations of migrant children at a time when the Trump administration was trying to accelerate their removal. Court hearings and asylum interviews for many unaccompanied minors have been moved up in recent months, even as questions have swirled about who would represent them, immigration attorneys said.

“Bridge contracts are Band-Aids that are not stopping the wound,” said Michelle Brané, a former Department of Homeland Security official who led the family reunification task force under the Biden administration. “They help for some, but are not enough, and are not a long-term solution.”

The vast majority of unaccompanied minors who entered the United States have since been released to relatives or other sponsors. A much smaller number of children remain in shelters overseen by the Health and Human Services Department. In July, an average of about 1,800 children were in federal custody, according to department data.

Many children arrived at the border without a parent, often fleeing persecution or other hardship in their countries.

Shaina Aber, the executive director of Acacia Center for Justice, which manages a network that has provided migrant children with legal services, said the administration’s current approach left them vulnerable.

“Unaccompanied children need independent, ethically tethered, experienced lawyers who know how to work with them in a child-friendly” way, she said in a statement.

The federal government is required under law to provide legal services to unaccompanied children who are often too young to understand their rights, ranging from presentations about their rights to direct legal representation. That work has typically been contracted out to nonprofits whose lawyers have extensive experience representing and helping migrant children.

The federal government had a multiyear contract with the Acacia Center, an advocacy group that managed a national network of nonprofits that provided representation. The Trump administration has repeatedly tried to halt funding for the groups, and only recently disbursed money it had withheld, following a federal court order.

The Acacia Center contract expired at the end of July. The center said it declined to sign a new contract because the Trump administration wanted it to share “confidential data about our young clients,” including unique identification numbers assigned by the Department of Homeland Security, and information about their immigration cases.

A Health and Human Services Department spokesperson said the administration was not requesting privileged, attorney-client information from the network, and had no intention of providing information it obtained to other government agencies.

The end of the Acacia Center’s contract set off a scramble among the nonprofits that had been providing legal representation. In an effort to prevent thousands of children from immediately losing access to lawyers, many groups have been fund-raising and relying on reserves to continue representing them.

Michael Lukens, the executive director of the Washington-based Amica Center for Immigrant Rights, said his nonprofit was continuing to represent about 850 unaccompanied minors, even though its federal funding had lapsed. Mr. Lukens said his group was able to do so in part because of the funding the administration recently disbursed.

Still, he and others warned that those efforts were not sustainable. Some nonprofits said they were trying to transfer cases to pro bono attorneys.

“It’ll be a catastrophe for the children. You will see mass deportations,” Mr. Lukens said. “They’re making it very hard to fight these cases when you have an attorney, let alone without one.”

It is unclear if the roughly 20,000 cases handled by the network will be transferred to the government and its new contractors. Several nonprofits said in interviews that they had not been contacted by the government or its new legal service providers about transferring cases.

The Health and Human Services Department said it was working with other legal service providers, including the nonprofit U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants, which is slated to provide unaccompanied children with lawyers through the end of December.

The department also awarded a $158 million contract for legal services to Our Rescue, the nonprofit. The contract has a “base period” of six months, running through early February, according to the department.

The deal has drawn intense scrutiny because the organization does not have extensive experience representing unaccompanied children in court.

Our Rescue said in a statement that it had “decades of experience supporting vulnerable children,” and that it welcomed the responsibility of working with unaccompanied minors to ensure they had access to qualified legal counsel.

The group was founded by Tim Ballard, a former Department of Homeland Security agent who was accused by multiple women of being a sex predator. In several lawsuits, they said that Mr. Ballard preyed on their desire to help trafficking victims, coercing or forcing them into sexual encounters as part of their undercover work, The New York Times reported in 2024. Mr. Ballard has insisted that he did not engage in misconduct. While the courts have dismissed some of the legal claims against Mr. Ballard, multiple lawsuits remain active.

Our Rescue said in a statement that Mr. Ballard was no longer affiliated with the organization, and had not been involved since he left in 2023.

Another potential legal provider identified by the administration ultimately declined to do the work.

The Health and Human Services Department said on Aug. 6 that it intended to award up to $150 million in a no-bid contract to Burke Law Group, a small Texas firm that appeared to have limited immigration law experience and was led by attorneys with ties to President Trump. But this week, the department officially said the firm decided not to apply for the grant.

Marcella Burke, who held top positions at the Interior Department and the Environmental Protection Agency during the first Trump administration, said she explored the possibility of her firm assembling a network of lawyers to provide services to about 700 children. But during discussions with the Health and Human Services Department, she said it “became clear that the government’s proposed structure was not workable.”

“I became involved for one reason: children, some extremely young and facing heartbreaking circumstances,” Ms. Burke said in a statement. “All discussions were preliminary, and I never sought or accepted a grant of any amount.”

Eric Schmitt contributed reporting. Alain Delaquérière contributed research.

item.title: Trump Threatens Economic Pain for Countries That Help Iran
item.description:
President Trump issued his latest threat in the war with Iran, vowing on Wednesday to impose “tremendous economic consequences” on countries that do business with Iran.

Mr. Trump did not specify in his social media post what actions he would take, and the White House did not immediately respond to questions on the matter. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned last week of “never before seen” measures to pressure Iran.

The president has previously backed away from threats of severe escalation in the war, which has inflicted significant damage to the world economy since the United States and Israel launched attacks in late February.

Without naming particular countries, Mr. Trump seemed to suggest that he could target nations such as China that buy Iranian oil. He referred to tactics that Iran has used to circumvent the extensive U.S. sanctions that it weathered for years before the war began.

Many neighboring countries in the Gulf region also have significant economic ties to Iran. The United Arab Emirates announced a total embargo on trade and transactions with Iran on Monday. The announcement came hours after a call from Mr. Trump to the Emirati leader, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed.

“ANY country that allows its financial institutions, businesses, airports, or government entities to provide any type of lifeline to Iran will itself face TREMENDOUS Economic Consequences,” Mr. Trump wrote on Wednesday. “Oil smuggling, swap lines, cash transfers, exchange houses, ship registries, front companies — It all needs to stop NOW. You know who you are.”

Mr. Trump asserted, as he has since the opening days of the war, that victory was just over the horizon, and that Iran was “on the ropes” and “hanging by a thread.” But analysts have said that Iran shows no signs of capitulating and may step up attacks on U.S. allies.

International sanctions on Iran helped lead to the 2015 nuclear deal, an agreement negotiated by President Barack Obama that tightly restricted Iran’s ambitions to develop a nuclear weapon in exchange for ending sanctions that had crippled its economy. Mr. Trump tore up that deal three years later and reimposed the sanctions, which pushed Iran into another severe economic crisis.

But in the wake of Mr. Trump reneging on the nuclear pact, Iran has adapted to the sanctions, developing sophisticated smuggling routes and new markets, particularly for oil. Iran’s economy is badly damaged, but its leaders have repeatedly asserted control in crackdowns on protests.

Esmail Baghaei, the spokesman for Iran’s foreign ministry, said on Monday that new measures would have “no effect on Iran’s position.”

]]>
